title: WHY DID MATTHEW COUNT TO FOURTEEN THREE TIMES? THE SECRET HIDING IN JESUS’ FAMILY TREE
paragraphs: WHY DID MATTHEW COUNT TO FOURTEEN THREE TIMES? THE SECRET HIDING IN JESUS’ FAMILY TREE

You may have skipped Matthew’s genealogy your entire life. But hidden inside those names is a message about kings, collapse, scandal, exile, grace—and a King who entered a broken family line to rewrite everything.
You open the Gospel of Matthew determined to read about Jesus.
Then you meet a wall of names.
Abraham begot Isaac. Isaac begot Jacob. Jacob begot Judah.
Maybe you quietly think, I already know where this is going.
You want the Sermon on the Mount.
But Matthew refuses to begin there.
Before he shows you Jesus healing the sick, forgiving sinners, confronting hypocrisy, calming storms, carrying a cross, and walking out of a grave...
Matthew gives you a family tree.
And then, almost as though he knows you might miss what he has done, he stops at Matthew 1:17 and essentially tells you:
Πᾶσαι οὖν αἱ γενεαὶ ἀπὸ Ἀβραὰμ ἕως Δαυὶδ γενεαὶ δεκατέσσαρες, καὶ ἀπὸ Δαυὶδ ἕως τῆς μετοικεσίας Βαβυλῶνος γενεαὶ δεκατέσσαρες, καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς μετοικεσίας Βαβυλῶνος ἕως τοῦ Χριστοῦ γενεαὶ δεκατέσσαρες.
All the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; from David to the Babylonian exile, fourteen; and from the exile to the Christ, fourteen.
Why would Matthew deliberately arrange the opening genealogy of Jesus into three groups built around the same number?
It was not because Israel's history naturally fell into three mathematically perfect blocks of fourteen biological generations.

Comparison with the Old Testament genealogical records shows that Matthew omits some names. For example, between Joram and Uzziah, the Old Testament records Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah. Ancient genealogies could be telescoped: “fathered” or “begot” could describe ancestral descent without requiring that every intervening generation be named. Matthew has therefore arranged his genealogy purposefully rather than attempting to provide an exhaustive modern-style family registry.
So Matthew is doing theology through genealogy.
He is telling you something before Jesus ever speaks.
And one of the strongest clues is sitting inside a Hebrew name.
Hebrew originally writes the name with the consonants:
In the traditional numerical values of Hebrew letters:

This connection between David's Hebrew name and Matthew's fourteen-generation structure has long been proposed by interpreters and is widely regarded as a compelling explanation of Matthew's arrangement, though we should distinguish that strong scholarly interpretation from something Matthew explicitly states. Matthew never writes, “I chose fourteen because David's Hebrew name equals fourteen.” Scholars infer the connection from the genealogy's structure, Matthew's extraordinary emphasis on David, and ancient numerical practices. Scholarly work continues to examine precisely how numerical composition operates in Matthew's genealogy.
But now go back to Matthew's first sentence.
Before the list even begins, he announces:
“the son of David, the son of Abraham.”
David is not buried somewhere deep inside the genealogy.
Matthew puts him at the front door.
Then he structures the genealogy around fourteen.
Then he explicitly calls David “the king” in Matthew 1:6.
Matthew is practically ringing a bell over the genealogy.
Matthew wants his readers to understand that the story they are entering is the story of the promised Messiah, the royal Son of David.
But there is something even more beautiful happening.
Because Matthew's three movements do not merely count people.
That is not merely somebody's ancestry.
That is the Gospel hiding inside a family tree.
And maybe that is why this genealogy feels strangely personal when you finally stop skipping it.
Because perhaps your life has had those movements too.
There was a season when everything seemed full of promise.
Maybe your marriage entered a place you never imagined.
Maybe an addiction became stronger than you wanted anyone to know.
Maybe you became excellent at looking Christian while privately becoming spiritually numb.
Maybe people know the version of you that smiles at church...
but they do not know the version of you that cries in the car.
They do not know what you search for when nobody is watching.
They do not know about the resentment.
The questions about God you are afraid to say aloud.
The prayer life that slowly disappeared.
The Bible collecting dust beside your bed.
The terrifying thought that sometimes whispers:
Maybe I have gone too far.
Matthew's genealogy has something to say to that person.
Because Jesus did not arrive at the end of a spotless family history.
And Matthew does something startling when he reaches Solomon.
He could simply have moved to the next generation.
Instead he reminds the reader that Solomon's mother had been “the wife of Uriah.”
Matthew refuses to airbrush David's history.
Behind that phrase stands one of the darkest episodes in David's life: Bathsheba, Uriah, adultery, abuse of royal power, deception, and bloodshed.

Matthew's genealogy also unusually draws attention to women including Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, “the wife of Uriah,” and finally Mary. Scholars have long debated precisely why Matthew selected these women, and reducing all of them simply to “scandalous women” is too simplistic; serious scholarship notes their varied situations, marginality, and important roles within the biblical story.
Matthew is not telling us that sin does not matter.
The Bible never calls darkness light.
Grace is not God pretending sin is harmless.
God enters a history damaged by sin...
That may be the message somebody reading this desperately needs.
Your worst chapter does not possess the authority to write the final chapter.
Matthew's genealogy begins with Abraham because God made promises.
It moves through David because God made promises.
It passes through exile because human failure did not cancel God's faithfulness.
after families had lived and died waiting...
after generations wondered whether God had forgotten...
The genealogy does not terminate in another political dynasty.
It arrives at ὁ Χριστός — ho Christos — the Christ, the Anointed One.
Christos is the Greek designation corresponding to “Messiah,” the Anointed One.
The genealogy has been moving toward Him.
The kings could not save us.
Religious ancestry could not save us.
Human achievement could not save us.
And suddenly those three fourteens become more than an interesting biblical pattern.
But failure does not have to be your final destination.
Your story may contain exile—the feeling that you have wandered so far from God that you barely recognize the person you have become.
But exile does not have to be the last word.
There is a name waiting at the end of Matthew's genealogy.
And there is a cross waiting at the end of Matthew's Gospel.
Jesus did not come merely to improve respectable people.
He came to call people to repentance.
He came to reconcile the guilty to God.
That is why Christianity is not ultimately the story of human beings climbing their way toward God.
It is the announcement that in Jesus Christ, God came to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
Maybe you have spent years editing your own genealogy.
You tell people the acceptable chapters.
You hide the night everything collapsed.
You hide what happened after everybody went to sleep.
You hide the person you became when grief changed you.
You hide because somewhere deep inside you believe that if people knew the entire story, they might walk away.
But Christ already knows the entire story.
And the Gospel still calls you toward Him.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
David was forgiven, yet his sin produced devastating consequences.
The cross itself tells us how costly sin is.
But the cross also tells us how far God was willing to go to redeem sinners.
So if this article has uncovered something you have been hiding, do not merely feel emotional for five minutes and continue living exactly the same way.
Seek reconciliation where Scripture requires it.
Not because typing a comment saves you.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
Let another believer know you need prayer.
Maybe somebody reading the comments has survived the valley you are walking through right now.
Maybe your honesty will become somebody else's permission to stop hiding.
And perhaps there is someone on your Facebook friends list who needs this genealogy more than you realized.
Not because they are fascinated by biblical numerology.
Because they believe their scandal has disqualified them from grace.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly but desperately needs to hear that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.

Because there may come a night when Babylon feels louder than Bethlehem, when failure feels stronger than promise, and you need to remember that Matthew deliberately carried the story through exile all the way to Christ.

We want this ministry to remain a place where Scripture is opened carefully, Jesus Christ remains central, sin is taken seriously, grace is never cheapened, and broken people are continually pointed toward repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation through the Gospel.
And never because anyone should pressure you into giving.
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ, μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης...
“Each one” should give according to what has been purposed in the heart, not reluctantly or “under compulsion”—ἐξ ἀνάγκης—because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7).
That is the spirit in which we invite your support.
Your support helps make continued Christian content, biblical teaching, discipleship materials, encouragement, and Gospel-centered resources possible.
Sometimes the person who cannot financially support a ministry can still help the truth travel farther than money ever could.
Because in the end, Gospel Warrior is not the hero of this story.
David certainly is not the hero.
Matthew begins his Gospel with generations of imperfect people because Christianity was never supposed to be a museum displaying perfect human beings.
It is the announcement of a perfect Savior entering a world of sinners.
And perhaps that is why Matthew's genealogy begins to feel less like a list once you understand it.
And at the end of all that waiting stands the One Matthew wanted you to see from his very first sentence:
So when you look at the wreckage behind you, remember this:
Babylon may appear in your history, but when Jesus takes hold of a repentant sinner, Babylon does not have to write the ending.
Because the genealogy Matthew expected people to remember was never merely about where Jesus came from.
It was announcing Who had finally come.
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your past—but the scars in Christ's hands declare that your sin does not have to own your ending.
